name: CT-RATE
description: A public open-source dataset pairing non-contrast 3D chest CT volumes with corresponding radiology text reports. CT-RATE comprises 25,692 scans from 21,304 unique patients and 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes, with over 14.3 million 2D slices. Each exam includes radiology report sections such as findings and impression, and the dataset also includes extracted multi-abnormality labels for 18 abnormalities and openly available anatomical segmentation labels.
creator: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci
citeAs: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci. CT-RATE: Paired chest CT volumes and radiology reports. https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibrahimhamamci/CT-RATE. 2025.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was curated from chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. It includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired between May 2015 and January 2023. Every reconstructed volume from the hospital database was incorporated to capture different reconstruction techniques. Reports were anonymized, translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API, and reviewed and corrected by bilingual final-year medical students. CT volumes were anonymized, standardized in orientation, and filtered to exclude contrast-enhanced volumes or body parts other than the chest.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Since the RAD-ChestCT dataset lacks a Mosaic attenuation label, it is excluded from external evaluation. Detailed metadata for the second external validation set (UPMC) is not publicly available because it is a private dataset and cannot be shared.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of chest CT volumes, associated metadata, and radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. The CT-RATE dataset contains the original raw data.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Reports were anonymized by removing personal information using targeted searches with regular expressions, then translated from Turkish to English with the Google Translate API and manually reviewed and corrected by bilingual final-year medical students. CT volumes were filtered to exclude contrast material and non-chest body parts, orientation was standardized using metadata, and identifying information was removed from metadata. Similar abnormalities were grouped during label creation, such as left and right mucoid impactions under mucoid impaction, various lung opacities under lung opacity, and lung and fissural nodules under lung nodules.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each CT volume was resized to uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in the x-axis and y-axis and 1.5 mm in the z-axis. Volumes were then center-cropped or padded to a consistent resolution of 480 × 480 × 240. CT volumes were converted to Hounsfield Unit values using intercept and slope values from metadata, clipped to the range -1000 to 1000, and normalized to -1 to 1 during training. Identical preprocessing was applied to external datasets for consistent evaluation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each CT exam is accompanied by a radiology report authored by a radiologist. For automated label extraction, 1,000 reports were manually annotated for 18 abnormalities by merging findings and impression sections; conditions not referenced in either section were considered absent. The annotated reports were split into training and validation sets and used to finetune the RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m model, which was then applied to classify the remaining 24,692 reports. In addition, organ-level anatomical segmentation labels were generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model. For CT-CHAT, over 2.7 million question-answer pairs were derived from CT-RATE using Llama 3.1 8B, and only accurately generated and properly formatted data that could be parsed as JSON were selected.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The finetuned report classifier's precision, recall, and F1 scores are reported for the 18 abnormalities, showing robust classification. For CT-CHAT VQA data, only accurately generated and properly formatted data that could be successfully parsed as JSON were retained for training. Expert evaluation of report generation was conducted by three board-certified radiologists who independently rated 150 reports per model.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Radiology reports: 1 report per CT exam authored by a radiologist; manual abnormality labels: 1 annotation per report for the 1,000 manually annotated reports; expert evaluation: 3 radiologist ratings per selected report
rai:annotatorDemographics: Bilingual final-year medical students reviewed and corrected translated reports and removed residual personal information. Three board-certified radiologists independently rated report-generation outputs; two were thoracic radiologists from Zurich and one was from Istanbul.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google Translate API, RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m, Llama 3.1 8B, TotalSegmentator
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly accessible via Hugging Face. The authors state that they plan to extend CT-RATE with multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels for 3D chest CT volumes as future work. Code and trained models are publicly available on GitHub.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Patient age, sex, clinical information, medical history, scan metadata, and radiology reports. The paper states that all chest CT volumes, associated metadata, and radiology text reports were anonymized before computational analysis.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset and associated models are intended to address critical challenges in 3D medical imaging, support future innovations in medical AI, improve patient care, reduce radiologists' workload, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and broaden accessibility through a user-friendly graphical interface for educational and clinical research settings.
rai:dataBiases: Biases inherent to the single-institution dataset may influence self-supervised training. Although the dataset is large and diverse, the data originate from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit generalizability to other populations. The paper also notes that CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection, and variability in disease descriptions across reports can affect detection accuracy.
rai:dataLimitations: CT-RATE is a single-center dataset, which may limit generalizability despite heterogeneity in scanners and protocols. Current models are limited to chest CT volumes only. CT-CLIP depends on report terminology and prompt choice. The evaluation of CT-CHAT is limited by the lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal baselines, requiring comparison to 2D models using DRRs and to 3D report-generation models. The quality of CT-CHAT's generated reports remains insufficient for clinical use, and the radiologists emphasized that substantial progress is still needed before clinical deployment. Challenges such as robustness, interpretability, regulatory compliance, and prospective validation remain.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for training and internal validation of CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT, for zero-shot multi-abnormality detection, supervised baseline training, finetuning, volume-to-volume retrieval, report-to-volume retrieval, visual question answering, and report generation. The cohort is split into training and validation sets, with 20,000 patients allocated to training and 1,304 to validation. The paper positions CT-RATE as an open-source resource for computational research in 3D medical imaging and future development of clinically deployable systems.
